Concussion

The 48-completer sham-controlled trial found no significant active-versus-sham difference in concussion symptoms at week 3 or week 6. One uncontrolled case report described improvement, and mouse studies reported physiological changes after repeated concussion.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

The 48-completer sham-controlled trial found no significant active-versus-sham difference in concussion symptoms at week 3 or week 6. One uncontrolled case report described improvement, and mouse studies reported physiological changes after repeated concussion.

Summary of the Evidence

The concussion category contains four unique titles: one randomized human trial, one human case report and two mouse publications. The mouse papers come from a related research program and model repeated concussion; because the records do not establish whether they used separate animal cohorts, they should not be treated as two independent replications. There are no reviews or independent clinical replications in this set.

Human and clinical evidence

Taylor et al. randomized adults with concussion to active or sham transcranial PBM. Forty-eight participants completed the six-week study. The groups did not differ significantly on the measured concussion symptom outcomes at week 3 or week 6 (Taylor et al. 2024). Chao et al. reported one person who used a home device after concussion and described changes over treatment and follow-up, but an uncontrolled case cannot separate treatment effects from natural recovery or other influences (Chao et al. 2020).

Animal evidence

Two 2026 mouse publications examine repeated concussion. One reports changes in cerebrovascular and meningeal-lymphatic measures after transcranial PBM, while another studies physiological effects in a multiple-concussion model. They provide biological findings rather than evidence of symptom recovery in people (Bragin et al. 2026 Kibria et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo concussion study was identified. Laboratory measures in the mouse papers remain part of those animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human trial used repeated transcranial near-infrared PBM over six weeks. The case report used home treatment with a different schedule. The database describes near-infrared wavelengths in the clinical reports, but does not provide a complete matching set of dose and exposure settings for comparison. The newer mouse studies used different injury models and physiological endpoints, so their procedures cannot be assumed to reproduce the human intervention.

Interpretation

The best direct evidence does not show symptom benefit from the tested six-week protocol. The case report and mouse findings identify questions for future work but do not overturn that controlled result. The main uncertainty is whether another dose, treatment window or patient subgroup could produce a clinically meaningful effect.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for symptom improvement with the studied six-week transcranial protocol Very low for other schedules
Publications and records4 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One completed sham-controlled trial directly tested concussion symptoms and found no group difference at either measured time point. A single home-treatment case cannot establish cause, while the two newer mouse reports measure mechanisms in a different setting. Replication should use larger trials, prespecified symptom and functional outcomes, and longer follow-up.
